uslaw-usc-t1-s112b:
Section 112b of Title 1 imposes transparency duties for international agreements. Not less often than once each month, the Secretary must provide a package in writing. The recipients are the majority and minority leaders of both Houses, the Speaker, and the appropriate congressional committees.

The package must list all international agreements signed, concluded, or finalized during the prior month. It must do the same for qualifying non-binding instruments. The text of each agreement and instrument must be included. A detailed description of the legal authority for each item must also be included. For an agreement, that authority is stated as the Secretary views it. For a non-binding instrument, the view of the department or agency in charge is given. The section sits in Chapter 2 of Title 1. The hosted Code is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s132b: Section 132b of Title 2 of the United States Code fixes the makeup of the Joint Committee of Congress on the Library. It sits in Chapter 5 of Title 2, on the Library of Congress, current through Public Law 119-134. On and after January 3, 1947, the Joint Committee consists of named Senate and House members. From the Senate come the chairman and four members of the Committee on Rules and Administration. From the House come the chairman and four members of the Committee on House Oversight.
uslaw-usc-t2-s142b:
Section 142b of Title 2 of the United States Code makes the Library of Congress's certifying officers answerable for their vouchers. A certifying officer approves payments from public funds. Since June 13, 1957, the section has fixed personal responsibility for that act.

The rule reaches every officer or employee duly authorized in writing by the Librarian. The Copyright Office is expressly included in the library's coverage. Such an officer is held responsible for the facts recited in the certificate. He answers for the facts stated on the voucher and its supporting papers too. He must also stand behind the legality of the payment under the fund charged. A third clause, kept in the text, holds him accountable for correct computations. One listed clause is marked repealed in the current text. The design is plain: public money moves only on the word of a named person who risks his own liability.
uslaw-usc-t2-s162b:
Section 162b of Title 2 covers employee benefits for staff of the Library of Congress child care center. The center is known as the Little Scholars Child Development Center. The section deals with pay and personnel matters for its workers. It lets a Center employee elect to be covered by its terms.

The election is made with the Librarian of Congress. It must be made within the windows the text sets, tied to the start of employment. A covered employee may be credited, under the retirement law of Title 5, for Center service before December 21, 2000. That credit depends on the employee paying the required deposit. The text also addresses qualification for survivor annuities and disability benefits. Contributions to the thrift savings plan and certification of creditable service are covered as well. The section sits in Chapter 5 of Title 2.
uslaw-usc-t2-s182b:
Section 182b of Title 2 establishes a revolving fund for Library of Congress services. The fund is established in the Treasury. It serves a list of programs and activities of the Librarian. They include decimal classification development and the operation of a gift shop or other sales tied to the Library's collections, exhibits, performances, and special events.

Document reproduction and microfilming services are on the list. Special events and programs, and training, complete it. A separate account must be kept in the fund for each listed program or activity. The Librarian may charge a fee for services under any of them. Fees charged are deposited into the account for that program or activity. The section then sets out what each account holds and how it may be used. It sits in Chapter 5 of Title 2.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1862b:
Section 1862b of Title 2 allows a money transfer between two House-side accounts. During fiscal year 2019 and each year after, funds for the Architect of the Capitol under the House Office Buildings heading may be moved. They may be transferred to the House of Representatives. There they merge with funds under the Allowances and Expenses heading.

A transfer needs the approval of the House Committee on Appropriations. Money moved keeps the same period of availability it had as an Architect appropriation. A yearly ceiling applies to the route. The aggregate amount transferred under the section in any fiscal year may not exceed a fixed sum stated in the text. That sum is thirty million dollars. The section sits in Chapter 28 of Title 2, in the subchapter on appropriations and expenditures. The hosted Code is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s282b:
Section 282b of Title 2 of the United States Code fixes the pay of the House's Legislative Counsel and his staff. The Legislative Counsel heads the office that drafts bills for the House of Representatives. His own salary is set by a comparison written into the section.

The Counsel is paid a yearly gross rate chosen by a greater-of test. One figure is a flat amount stated in the text, 173,900 dollars. The other is the rate in effect under an order of the Speaker issued under section 4532. Whichever rate is greater governs his pay. Staff members of the office are paid at rates the Counsel fixes. Those rates need the Speaker's approval, or must follow policies the Speaker approved. A ceiling ties staff pay to an applicable limit named later in the text. The section joins a professional drafting office to the Speaker's control of the purse.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2b: Section 2b of Title 2 of the United States Code sets House seats by state. Each state is to have the count shown in a named statement. That statement was sent to Congress on the 8th of January 1941. It rests on a method called the method of equal proportions. The count holds from the Seventy-eighth Congress onward by the text. It holds till a new split under a later law takes effect. No state is to get less than one Member in the House.
